summary:
Guanajuato stands within Mexico's state-by-state system for legal gender recognition. As of March 2025, 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operate one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted nothing, and only seven states extend recognition to children. The Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. Which of these applies in Guanajuato is not stated in the sources reviewed here.

Human Rights Watch documents incidents recorded in Guanajuato, alongside Tabasco, of identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market where no recognition procedure exists. For a trans visitor, the practical exposure sits where identification is checked: medical care, schooling-related dealings and any encounter in which the document presented does not correspond to the person's presentation.

Guanajuato has no transfemicide statute of its own in the sources reviewed. The national benchmark for lethal violence against trans people is set by two states: Nayarit, which criminalised transfemicide in 2022 with a penalty of up to 60 years, and Mexico City, whose 'Paola Buenrostro law' of July 2024 raised the penalty to up to 70 years. In 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, and impunity for transfemicide is thought to be higher still.
tangentialFactors:
Impunity is the operative condition rather than the statute alone. In 2022 more than 95% of homicides across Mexico went unpunished, and the Guardian reported that impunity for transfemicide is thought to exceed that figure. A transfemicide law in a neighbouring state therefore offers a trans visitor in Guanajuato no practical protection.

Two of Mexico's 32 states have enacted transfemicide statutes, in Nayarit and Mexico City. Guanajuato is not among them on the evidence reviewed, so lethal violence against a trans person here would be prosecuted, if at all, under ordinary homicide provisions without the aggravating finding.
localsOnly:
Residents of Guanajuato who need legal gender recognition must use whatever administrative procedure the state provides, if any; the sources reviewed do not state whether Guanajuato has enacted one. Where no procedure exists, residents carry identity documents that contradict their presentation, which Human Rights Watch records as driving discrimination in Guanajuato's schools, medical clinics and labour market.

Residents facing lethal violence have no transfemicide charge available under Guanajuato law on this evidence, unlike residents of Nayarit and Mexico City. The national homicide impunity rate of more than 95% in 2022 applies to cases prosecuted here.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Guanajuato has enacted an administrative gender-recognition procedure, and its status among the 22 states that had done so as of March 2025, is unresolved in the sources reviewed. The inventory places Guanajuato among jurisdictions where HRW documented consequences of absent recognition, but does not confirm the state's legislative position.

Guanajuato's own hate-crime provisions, police practice toward trans people, and availability of gender-affirming care are not sourced here and remain unverified. The transfemicide penalties cited belong to Nayarit and Mexico City and are not Guanajuato law.
